en: I bow down to that primordial Lord,
by whom the science of Haṭhayoga was taught,
which shines forth as the exalted Royal Yoga (Rājayoga).
Like a ladder for one desiring to ascend. Once, Caṇḍakāpālin went to the hermitage of Gheraṇḍa.
Having bowed with humility and devotion,
he questioned Gheraṇḍa. Caṇḍakāpāli said:
O Lord of Yoga, the yoga residing within the jar is the cause of the knowledge of reality;
I now desire to hear about it.
"O Lord, speak of Yoga-Īśvara. Gheraṇḍa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one!"
That which you ask me,
I shall indeed tell you in truth; listen with focused attention.
There is no snare equal to illusion;
there is no power superior to yoga;
for there is no kinsman higher than knowledge.
There is no enemy more formidable than the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra).
Through the practice of [meditating on] the letters beginning with *ka*,
one may come to understand the scriptures as they truly are.
Likewise, having attained yoga, the knowledge of reality is obtained through well-performed and ill-performed actions. //1.5// [1.6.1] Through well-performed and ill-performed deeds.
The jar is produced from living beings;
from the jar, action arises;
just as the jar-machine revolves. //1.6//
Just as a water-wheel moves up and down by the power of oxen,
so too does the individual soul move by the power of karma.
It wanders through birth and death,
like an unbaked clay jar situated in water,
a vessel that is constantly wearing away.
Having thoroughly incinerated [the vessel] with the fire of yoga,
one should perform the purification of the jar.
Purification and firmness indeed [constitute this process].
Stability, fortitude, and lightness;
direct perception and non-attachment—
these are the seven means residing within the jar.
Purification is achieved through the six actions;
firmness arises through posture;
stability is attained through the *mudrās*, and steadfastness through withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*).
From breath control (prāṇāyāma) comes lightness;
from meditation (dhyāna), direct perception of the Self within oneself; and from concentration (samādhi), freedom from attachment.
Liberation itself [is attained], there is no doubt.
1.11 Dhauti, Vasti, as well as Neti, Laulikī, and likewise Trāṭaka. 1.12–13a
<1.12/2> Kapālabhāti and these [others]— one should perform these six practices. <1.13/1> Internal cleansing (Antardhauti) and dental cleansing (Dantadhauti).
Heart-washing (*hṛt-dhauti*) is the purification of the root. Dhauti is said to be of four kinds; it makes the vessel stainless. (1.13)
The essence of the wind, the essence of the water,
and the essence of the fire have been cast outside for the sake of making the jar free from impurity.
Internal dhauti is of four kinds:
one should drink air very slowly through the mouth, like the beak of a crow.
One should then agitate the abdomen and slowly exhale through the path of the nose. This is the supreme *vātasāra*, which must be kept strictly secret.
It makes the body free from impurities,
it causes the destruction of all diseases,
and it increases the digestive fire of the body.
One should fill the water up to the throat and drink it slowly through the mouth;
one should then move it about within the abdomen itself.
And one should exhale from the abdomen downward. This essence of water is supremely secret;
it is that which purifies the body of its impurities.
He who accomplishes this with effort attains the body of a god;
[he attains] the supreme purification, the essence of water.
He who accomplishes this with diligence,
having purified the body of impurities,
attains the divine body.
One should perform [this practice] one hundred times upon the navel-knot at the back of Mount Meru;
having abandoned the disease arising from the stomach, [one attains health].
It increases the digestive fire;
this *dhauti* is the essence of fire,
bestowing the perfection of yoga upon practitioners.
This dhauti is supreme and must be kept secret; it should never be disclosed.
By dhauti alone— [the goal is attained].
Having accomplished the *kākīmudrā*, one should certainly fill the great belly; [then] the body of a god will surely come to be. //1.21// <1.22/1>
One should hold [the breath] for half a watch (one hour and a half),
then move it through the downward path;
this *dhauti* is supremely secret.
It should never be made manifest.
Standing with the navel submerged in water,
one should cleanse the channel of power (śakti-nāḍī).
One should wash the urethra with both hands until the discharge of impurities occurs;
having thus washed the urethra, [one should proceed].
One should place it back into the belly.
This cleansing method is secret;
it is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
Merely by means of *dhauti* alone,
the body of a god will certainly be attained. As long as a person does not master the power of *ardha-dhāraṇā*, [the divine body is not achieved].
The great dhautī, when performed externally,
does not arise at all. [It begins] at the root of the teeth and the root of the tongue.
The two cavities of the ears and the cavity of the skull—
these five [are the locations] where the cleansing of the teeth is prescribed. //1.26//
Then, with the sap of the *khadira* tree and with pure clay,
one should cleanse the roots of the teeth.
It should be done until all impurity has been removed. 1.27.
For yogins practicing the means of yoga, *dhauti* performed beyond the roots of the teeth is supreme. 1.28.1.
The practitioner of yoga should always perform the cleansing of the teeth at dawn;
the root of the teeth is the foundation for concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and the other [limbs of yoga].
Because [this is] for the sake of the tasks of yogins... 1.28 / Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the means for the purification of the tongue. 1.29.
The *dīrghalambikā* [mudrā] destroys old age, death, disease, and so forth.
[It is formed by] the index, middle, and ring fingers.
By joining three fingers,
one should insert them into the middle of the throat and cleanse the impurity of the uvula.
Having cleansed it very gradually,
one should ward off the disorder of phlegm;
one should cleanse it with fresh butter.
And one should milk it again and again;
having repeatedly drawn out that essence with an iron instrument, [one should process it]. //1.31//
One should always perform this with effort at sunrise and at sunset; for when the daily rite has been performed in this manner, [the goal is attained].
The uvula has become elongated;
by joining the tips of the index fingers,
one should cleanse the two ear canals.
Through constant practice of yoga, the manifestation [of the inner sound] occurs within the resonance (*nāda*). With the right thumb pressed against the [ear], [one hears it]. 1.33–34.1.
One should rub the aperture of the forehead;
by means of such practice,
one shall ward off the disorder of phlegm.
The channels become free from impurity,
and divine vision arises at the end of sleep and at the end of eating.
And at the end of the day, every single day,
one should perform the threefold cleansing of the heart by means of the staff, the emetic, and clothing.
Having moved a plantain stalk, a green stalk,
and likewise a cane stalk across the middle of the heart;
One should withdraw [the breath] slowly again; likewise, one should expel phlegm, bile,
and moisture through the upward path.
By means of the procedure for *daṇḍadhauti*,
one will certainly destroy diseases of the heart. At the end of a meal, one should drink water.
Having drawn [the water] up to the ears, the wise one should gaze upward for a moment and then spit out that water again.
One should constantly ward off phlegm and bile through the practice of yoga. Nineteen cubits [is the measurement].
Likewise, twenty-five [finger-breadths] in length and four finger-breadths in width,
one should slowly swallow a fine cloth.
One should draw this back again;
this is proclaimed as the practice of *dhauti*.
It cures abdominal tumors, fever, splenic disorders, and leprosy.
Kapha and pitta are destroyed;
health, strength, and nourishment shall accrue to him day by day. (1.41)
The impurity of the downward breath (apāna) persists as long as its root has not been purified;
therefore, one should strive with every effort.
One should perform the purification of the root with the stalk of the *pītāmūla* plant, or even with the middle finger. 1.42–1.43.1.
One should diligently wash the private parts with water again and again;
one should prevent the hardness of the abdomen.
It wards off undigested food and that which has been digested;
it is the cause of beauty and nourishment,
and it stimulates the circle of the digestive fire.
There are two types of enemas known: the liquid enema (jala-vasti) and the dry enema (śuṣka-vasti).
One should administer the liquid enema in water.
Always with a dry bladder on the ground,
with the anus submerged in water,
he sits in the utkaṭa posture with the nozzle inserted into the rectum.
One should practice contraction and expansion,
and employ the *jala-vasti* (water enema). This cures urinary disorders (*prameha*) and prolapse of the rectum (*gudāvarta*).
One should ward off the cruel wind;
one's body shall become subject to one's own will,
and one shall become equal to Kāmadeva.
Having gently moved the bladder backward,
one should [apply] the anus with the Aśvinī mudrā.
One should contract and expand [the abdomen].
By practicing in this manner through yoga,
no disorder of the internal cavity (koṣṭha-doṣa) occurs.
It increases the digestive fire and destroys undigested wind (āmavāta).
[One should use] a fine thread measuring one span (vitasti) in length.
One should cause it to enter through the stalk of the nose and then cause it to exit from the mouth;
this is declared to be the *neti* practice.
By means of this practice, one attains the accomplishment of Khecarī; even through the performance of ritual action, one does not [fail],
and the defects of phlegm (kapha) are destroyed.
Divine vision arises.
One should rotate the abdomen with moderate speed on both sides.
It destroys all diseases here and increases the digestive fire of the body,
provided one abandons even the blinking of the eyes.
One should gaze at a subtle object until tears fall;
this is called *trāṭaka* by the wise. (1.53)
Thus, through the yoga of practice,
the Śāmbhavī [mudrā] certainly arises;
no disease of the eyes occurs.
It bestows divine vision.
[This occurs] by means of the leftward sequence, the reverse sequence,
and especially by the cooling sequence.
One should illuminate the forehead and divide [the breath] into three parts;
this wards off the disorder of phlegm (kapha).
One should fill the air through the *iḍā* and then exhale it through the *piṅgalā*.
Having filled [with breath] by means of Piṅgalā,
one should again exhale by means of Candrā.
Having performed inhalation and exhalation, [one should proceed].
One should not move [the tongue] with force;
thus, through the practice of yoga,
one should ward off the disorder of phlegm.
Having drawn water through both nostrils,
one should exhale it again through the mouth;
if one performs this repeatedly, [it is known as] pāyampāyam.
One should eliminate the disorder of phlegm by drinking [the medicine] cold through the mouth,
or by inducing purgation through the nostrils.
Thus, through the yoga of practice,
one becomes equal to the gods of the desire realm;
neither birth nor old age occurs.
Fever shall not arise at all;
one may possess a body that acts according to one's own will,
and one shall ward off the disorder of phlegm.

Thus ends the first instruction, titled "The Means for Accomplishing the Six Actions," within the Yoga of the Pot (Ghaṭasthayoga) in the dialogue between Gheraṇḍa and Caṇḍa, from the venerable *Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā*. 1.61.0.1.
Gheraṇḍa said:
All postures (āsanas) are as numerous as there are living beings.
<2.1/2> Eighty-four hundred thousand [verses] were spoken by Śiva in the past. <2.2/1> Among those, the most distinguished are as follows:
One hundred minus sixteen was made;
among them, in the world of mortals,
there were thirty-two auspicious seats.
The *padma*, the *bhadra*,
the *mukta*, the *vajra*, and the *svastika*; the *siṃha*, the *gomukha*, and the *vīra*.
And likewise the bow-posture (dhanur-āsana); the hidden (gupta), the fish (mātsya),
and the king of fish-posture (matsyendra-āsana).
<2.4/2> Cow-guarding [posture], supine, and likewise with the buttocks raised and the knees together.
<2.5/1> Peacock, cock, and tortoise;
Likewise, [the postures] are: the upturned tortoise, the upturned frog, the tree, the frog, the garuḍa, and the bull. //2.5//
The locust, the crocodile, the camel,
the lizard, and the yogic posture—
these indeed are the thirty-two postures.
And it bestows perfection in the world of mortals.
(2.6) Pressing the base of one foot against the perineum, and having firmly pressed the other ankle against it,
then placing the chin upon the genitals and fixing the gaze upon the heart— (2.7)
<2.7/2> Standing firm like a pillar with the senses restrained, gazing with an unmoving vision at the space between the eyebrows—
<2.7/3> this is declared to be the Siddhāsana, which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation.
<2.8/1> Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh, and likewise the left [foot] upon the right;
Having firmly placed the two hands behind the thighs according to the prescribed method,
and having set the two thumbs upon the heart, one should gaze at the tip of the nose while looking at the chin;
this is called the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), which destroys the transformations of disease.
The two ankles are placed below the scrotum in reverse order; the two big toes are likewise joined with the two hands.
Having placed [the hands] upon the back [of the other],
and having reached the *jāladhara* [joint],
one should gaze at the tip of the nose.
This is the Bhadrasana (Auspicious Posture),
which destroys all diseases.
[In this posture,] the left ankle is placed at the root of the anus.
Placing the right ankle upon the body at the level of the head and neck is the liberated posture (muktāsana), which bestows success.
Having positioned the two shanks like a thunderbolt (vajra) with both feet beside the anus,
this shall be the vajrāsana posture.
Bestowing success upon yogins:
having placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs, the yogi [should remain]. 2.12–13.1.
Sitting with the body straight, that is called the Svastika posture. Placing the two ankles below the scrotum...
Having ascended upwards in reverse order,
they are established at the base of the *citi* and on the ground;
and the two hands are above the knees.
With the mouth slightly open and gazing at the tip of the nose,
this shall be the lion posture (siṃhāsana).
It destroys all diseases.
(2.15) Placing both feet firmly on the ground, one should rest them against the sides of the back. (2.16)
Having assumed a steady body,
with the face of a cow and the form of a cow’s mouth;
then, with one foot upon one [spot].
One should place [the foot] resting upon the thigh;
likewise on the other [thigh] afterwards.
This is declared to be the *vīrāsana* (hero’s posture).
Having stretched out the two feet on the ground like staffs,
and having placed the hands on the back with the pair of feet held [there],
one should make the body bent like a bow.
That which is called the bow-posture (*dhanur-āsana*) is indeed that. Lying on one's back upon the ground like a corpse is the corpse-posture (*śava-āsana*).
The corpse posture (śavāsana) removes fatigue and is the cause of mental rest. [2.19] The feet are placed between the knees and the thighs. [2.20]
Having crossed the feet, one should conceal them;
having placed one foot upon the other,
they know this to be the "secret posture" (guptāsana).
Having assumed the *muktapadma* posture,
one should lie on one's back;
then, encircling the head with both elbows.
The fish posture (matsyāsana), however, destroys disease.
Having performed a backward stretch upon the abdomen, one remains there with effort.
One should place the left foot with its limb bent upon the right knee; there,
one should also place the right elbow.
With the face turned toward the right hand,
the gaze directed between the eyebrows—
this is called the Matsyendra-pīṭha.
The two feet, with palms facing upward and clearly positioned, are placed between the knees and thighs;
and the two ankles are covered by the hands.
Having carefully turned [the feet] upward and constricted the throat,
one should gaze at the tip of the nose.
They say that the "cow-protection" posture (*gorakṣāsana*) is the cause of success for yogins. Extending both legs upon the ground like two staffs—
With the forehead resting between the two funeral pyres and the feet firmly held by both hands with effort,
they call this the "Yogendra-pīṭha" in the western reclining posture.
Pressing the earth with the two big toes and the two ankles raised toward the sky,
one should place the anus above them.
The *utkaṭāsana* (raised-seat posture) should be understood as follows:
having placed the root of the left foot upon the surface of the earth, [one sits] with the mind focused. 2.27–28.1.
With the southern foot-staff,
one should encircle the left foot;
the two hands should be placed upon the pair of knees.
This is the Saṃkaṭa posture (2.28). Having supported the earth with both hands,
the sides of the navel are placed upon the elbows (2.29).
Standing like a staff in the sky upon a high seat—
this they call the Peacock posture (mayūra-pīṭha).
Having consumed a great deal of food, one should reduce it all to ashes.

It generates the digestive fire in the stomach and would digest even *kālakūṭa* poison; it removes all diseases along with their remnants, such as abdominal tumors (*gulma*), fever, and the like. Indeed, the *śrīmayūra* posture becomes free from defects.
Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) with the hands placed between the knees and the thighs, one sits with the elbows [resting against the body].
Seated upon a couch, one assumes the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana). The two ankles are placed below the scrotum, positioned crosswise and held steady.
With the body, head, and neck held straight,
it is called the tortoise posture (*kūrma-āsana*). One should remain established in the binding of the cock posture (*kukkuṭa-āsana-bandha*).
Holding the neck with both hands, with the back of the head turned upward like a tortoise on its shell—
this is the *uttānakūrma* (upward-tortoise) posture.
One should touch the soles of the feet, the region of the back, and the two big toes; having placed the pair of knees forward.
One should practice the frog posture (maṇḍūkāsana). In the bound frog posture,
the head is supported by both elbows.
This is the "frog-like" (bhekavat) supine posture;
this is the supine frog (uttānamaṇḍuka).
And [it is performed] at the region of the root of the left thigh.
Having placed the right foot upon the ground,
he stands like a tree;
this they know as the tree posture (vṛkṣāsana).
Pressing the earth with the calves and thighs,
with the body steady and the two knees [together],
the pair of hands should be placed above the knees.
The Garuḍāsana is described as follows:
[place] the root of the anus upon the right ankle; on the left side, place the other foot.
If one touches the ground with the hands in the reverse manner,
this becomes the Bull Pose (*vṛṣāsana*). Having sat upon it, one lies down with the pair of feet upon the chest.
Pressing the ground with both hands,
with the feet [extended] one span above the void,
the lords of sages call this the *śalabha* posture.
Having placed his heart within it, he lies reclining upon it;
his two feet are extended upon the ground,
and his head is supported by the pair of his staff-like arms.
That is the makarāsana, which takes the form of a body-fire;
having sat upon it, one lies with both feet drawn in,
resting them upon the back while they are supported by the two hands.
Having properly contracted the abdomen, the mouth, and the cheeks,
ascetics call this the "camel" (*uṣṭra*) and the "seat" (*pīṭha*).
[The breath] extends from the big toe to the navel.
And one should place [the hands] on the ground below;
having supported the earth with the palms of both hands,
the head is held high like that of a serpent.
The fire within the body increases constantly;
it is the destroyer of all diseases.
The goddess Bhujaṅgī remains ever awake.
From the practice [of this], there arises the arm-posture (*bhujāsanam*).
Having placed the two feet face upwards and having positioned them upon the knees— //2.43–2.44//1//— [this is the posture].
Having placed the pair of hands face upward upon the seat,
one should draw in the breath with full inhalations.
One should not look at the tip of the nose;
this shall be the yoga posture for yogins in the practice of yoga.
[2.46/0] Thus ends the second instruction, titled "The Practice of Postures" within the *Ghaṭasthayoga*, from the *Śrī Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā*, in the dialogue between Gheraṇḍa and Caṇḍa.
[3.1/1] Gheraṇḍa said:
Mahāmudrā and Nabhomudrā.
Uḍḍīyāna is the water-bearer;
Mūlabandha and Mahābandha, as well as Mahāvedha and Khecarī. //3.1//
The *viparītakaraṇī* posture,
the *vajrolī*, the *śakticālanī*,
the *taḍāgī*, and the *māṇḍūkī* mudrā.
The five *dhāraṇās* of Śāmbhavī are Aśvinī, Pāśinī, Kākī, Mātaṅgī, and Bhujamginī. 3.2–3.3.1.
<3.3/2> And there are twenty-five mudrās,
which bestow accomplishment upon yogins here. <3.4/1> O Goddess, this is the chapter on mudrās.
This has been told in your presence;
by the mere knowledge of which,
all success is produced.
It should be guarded with great effort and must not be given to just anyone;
it bestows joy upon the yogins alone.
Having firmly pressed the root of the anus against the left ankle with great effort, [one should perform] the "durt" [posture], which possesses the splendor of the Maruts. //3.5// <3.6/1>
Then, having extended the right leg and grasped the toes of that foot with both hands,
one should perform the contraction of the throat.
One should gaze at the space between the eyebrows;
having filled the breath with inhalations,
it is called the Mahāmudrā.
It wards off wrinkles and graying hair, as well as old age and death; it cures consumption,
cough, and hemorrhoids.
Through the practice of Mahāmudrā, one shall destroy enlarged spleen, chronic fever, as well as all diseases. (3.8)
Wherever the yogi may be situated at all times in all his activities,
he should remain steady with his tongue turned upward.
One should always retain the breath;
this is the *nabhaḥ-mudrā*,
which destroys the diseases of yogins.
<3.10/1> One should perform the posterior extension on the abdomen, but one should carry it upward from the navel.
<3.10/2> Because it causes [the breath] to fly upward (uḍḍīna).
The great sky-traveler is fully rested;
this is the Uḍḍīyāna bandha,
the lion that slays the elephant of death.
Indeed,
this Uḍḍīyāna is superior to all other bonds;
when Uḍḍīyāna is thoroughly practiced, [it grants liberation].
Liberation would become natural.
Having performed the contraction of the throat,
one should place the chin upon the heart.
When the net-binding is performed,
it is the binding of the sixteen supports;
this is the great mudrā of the net-holder.
It causes the destruction of death;
it is the perfected Jālandhara-bandha,
which bestows success upon yogins.
Whoever practices this for six months indeed becomes perfected; of this there is no doubt.
[One should press] with the heel of the left foot...
Then, the wise practitioner should contract the *yoni* and, with great effort, press the knot of the navel against the spinal column (*merudaṇḍa*).
One should perform a firm binding of the penis with the right ankle,
both above and below the navel.
One should perform that with effort;
this is the mudrā that destroys old age,
which is called the root-lock (mūlabandha).
The man who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra should remain well-concealed in a secluded place.
One should practice this mudrā. Through the practice of this binding, the accomplishment of the vital wind (marut) will certainly occur. //3.16-3.17//1//
Then, one who is silent and has conquered laziness should diligently accomplish it by means of the ankle of the left foot.
The wise man should diligently press the root of the anus with the ankle of his right foot. //3.18//2//
One should move the heel very slowly;
one should contract the vagina slowly;
one should hold the breath in the *jālandhara* [bandha].
It is called the Great Bond (mahābandha).
The Great Bond is the supreme bond;
it is the destroyer of old age and death.
Through the grace of this bond,
one shall accomplish every desire:
beauty, youth, and loveliness.
For women, [the practice] without a man;
likewise, the *mūlabandha* and *mahābandha* without the *mahāvedha*. (3.21)
Having attained the great bond (mahābandha),
one should practice the upward-flying breath-retention (uḍḍāna-kumbhaka).
This is declared to be the Great Piercing (Mahāvedha),
which bestows accomplishment upon yogis.
[Next are] the Great Lock (Mahābandha) and the Root Lock (Mūlabandha).
He who performs this daily, endowed with the great piercing (*mahāvedha*),
is a yogi, the best among those who know yoga.
For him there is no fear of death,
nor does old age exist for him;
he should be protected with great effort.
Piercing that which is [attained] by yogis and bull-like men—
having severed the channel below the tongue,
one should constantly move the tongue.
One should milk [the plant] with fresh butter and extract [the essence] using an iron apparatus.
Thus, through constant practice, [the result is achieved].
The lambikā should reach length until it arrives at the middle of the eyebrows; then Khecarī is perfected. One should [place] the tongue in the middle of the palate.
One should gradually insert the tongue into the cavity of the skull,
having turned it back.
When the gaze is fixed between the two eyebrows,
it becomes the Khecarī Mudrā. There is neither fainting, nor hunger, nor thirst.
Neither does laziness arise,
nor do disease, old age, or death;
he attains the body of a god.
Fire does not burn his body;
the wind does not wither it;
and the waters do not moisten his frame.
One should not bite the arm;
[rather, it should be done on the thigh]. There will be beauty in the body, and meditative absorption (samādhi) will certainly arise.
When the skull and the mouth are joined, the tongue shall obtain the flavor. [3.30] That which arises from various methods [is to be experienced]. [3.31]
And day by day, [the food] becomes increasingly pleasant;
at first it is salty and alkaline,
and thereafter it becomes bitter and astringent.
Freshly drawn milk, clarified butter,
[cow's] milk, curd, buttermilk, and honey;
as well as grape juice and the first milk of a cow after calving.
From the tongue, water is produced.
The sun resides at the root of the navel,
and the moon at the root of the palate.
The sun devours the immortal;
thereafter, man falls under the power of death. One should therefore direct the sun upward.
And one should bring the moon down;
this is the Mudrā that performs the reversal,
hidden in all tantras.
Having placed his head upon the ground, with his two hands joined in composure,
he remains steady with his feet pointing upward.
This mudrā, considered the "reverser," should always be practiced; it shall accomplish [the goal] and destroy both old age and death. //3.35// <3.36/1>
He is perfected in all worlds; even at the time of dissolution, he does not perish. Having attained the perfected posture (siddhāsana), [he remains steadfast].
One should hold [the breath] at the ears, eyes, nose,
and mouth with the thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger, and so forth. (3.37)
Having drawn up the prāṇa with the "crow-like" [breathing], one should then join it with the apāna;
